studies.Reference: Soy, isoflavones, and breast cancer risk in Japan.
studies.Authors: Yamamoto S, Sobue T, Kobayashi M, Sasaki S, Tsugane S,
studies.Journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Consumption of miso soup and isoflavones was assessed using a self-administered questionnaire.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: 21 852 Japanese female residents (aged 40-59 years) from four public health center areas completed a self-administered questionnaire.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: The adjusted RRs for breast cancer for women in the highest quartile were 0.46 (95% CI = 0.25 to 0.84).
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Consumption of miso soup and isoflavones was inversely associated with the risk of breast cancer.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: 179 women were diagnosed with breast cancer.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Consumption of miso soup and isoflavones, but not of soyfoods, was inversely associated with the risk of breast cancer.

studies.Reference: Consumption of fermented milk products and breast cancer: a case-control study in The Netherlands.
studies.Authors: van't Veer P, Dekker JM, Lamers JW, Kok FJ, Schouten EG, Brants HA, Sturmans F, Hermus RJ
studies.comparison_type: High vs None (≥225 g/day vs None)
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: We observed a significantly lower consumption of fermented milk products (predominantly yogurt and buttermilk) among 133 incident breast cancer cases as compared to 289 population controls.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: 133 incident breast cancer cases as compared to 289 population controls.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: The age-adjusted odds ratio of daily consumption of 1.5 glasses (greater than or equal to 225 g) of fermented milk versus none was 0.50.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: These results support the hypothesis that high consumption of fermented milk products may protect against breast cancer.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Fermented milk products (predominantly yogurt and buttermilk)

studies.Reference: Soya foods and breast cancer risk: a prospective study in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan.
studies.Authors: Key TJ, Sharp GB, Appleby PN, Beral V, Goodman MT, Soda M, Mabuchi K
studies.comparison_type: consumption five or more times per week relative to consumption once a week or less
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Women completed dietary questionnaires in 1969-1970 and/or in 1979-1981

extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: The risk for breast cancer was not significantly associated with consumption of soya foods
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: for tofu, relative risks ... for consumption five or more times per week, relative to consumption once a week or less

studies.Reference: Cabbage and Sauerkraut Consumption in Adolescence and Adulthood and Breast Cancer Risk among US-Resident Polish Migrant Women.
studies.Authors: Pathak DR, Stein AD, He JP, Noel MM, Hembroff L, Nelson DA, Vigneau F, Shen T, Scott LJ, Charzewska J, Wajszczyk B, Clark K, Rybaczyk LA, Pathak BA, Błaszczyk D, Bankowski A, Willett WC
studies.Journal: International journal of environmental research and public health
studies.comparison_type: High adolescent and adult consumption vs Low adolescent and adult consumption
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Food frequency questionnaires assessed diet during adulthood and age 12-13 years.

extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Greater consumption of total and raw/short-cooked cabbage/sauerkraut foods either during adolescence or adulthood was associated with significantly reduced BC risk.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: Cases were 20-79 years old with histological/cytological confirmation of invasive BC.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Consumption of total, raw/short-cooked, and long-cooked cabbage/sauerkraut foods was categorized as low, medium, or high (frequency of servings/week).

studies.Reference: Long-term consumption of non-fermented and fermented dairy products and risk of breast cancer by estrogen receptor status - Population-based prospective cohort study.
studies.Authors: Kaluza J, Komatsu S, Lauriola M, Harris HR, Bergkvist L, Michaëlsson K, Wolk A
studies.comparison_type: High intake (≥3 servings/day) vs Low intake (<1 serving/day)
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Long-term consumption of dairy products was assessed using a self-administered food-frequency questionnaire in 1987 and 1997.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: The population-based Swedish Mammography Cohort included 33,780 women.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Consumption of fermented dairy products was inversely associated with ER-/PR- breast cancer (for consistently high intake ≥3 vs. <1 servings/day HR = 0.28).
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Consumption of fermented dairy products was inversely associated with ER-/PR- breast cancer.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: During 16.6 years of follow-up (559,286 person-years), 1870 total breast cancer cases were diagnosed (1162 ER+/PR+; 195 ER-/PR-).
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Consumption of fermented dairy products was assessed using a self-administered food-frequency questionnaire.

studies.Reference: Usual Consumption of Specific Dairy Foods Is Associated with Breast Cancer in the Roswell Park Cancer Institute Data Bank and BioRepository.
studies.Authors: McCann SE, Hays J, Baumgart CW, Weiss EH, Yao S, Ambrosone CB
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Intakes of dairy foods were queried with a self-administered food-frequency questionnaire.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Archived clinical and questionnaire data were obtained from the DBBR from 1941 women diagnosed with breast cancer between December 2003 and October 2014, and 1237 control participants.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Higher intakes of yogurt were associated with reduced risk of breast cancer (OR: 0.61; 95% CI: 0.46, 0.82).
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Higher intakes of yogurt were associated with reduced risk of breast cancer.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: The purpose of this study was to examine associations between the types and quantity of dairy foods consumed and the risk of breast cancer.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Intakes of dairy foods were queried with a self-administered food-frequency questionnaire and grouped into monthly intakes of total dairy, milk, yogurt, low-fat cheese, other cheese, and sweet dairy.

studies.Reference: Combination of dietary factors in relation to breast-cancer occurrence.
studies.Authors: Van 't Veer P, van Leer EM, Rietdijk A, Kok FJ, Schouten EG, Hermus RJ, Sturmans F
studies.comparison_type: High intake of fermented milk products and fiber vs Low intake
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Dietary factors were classified according to their possible mechanism of action, i.e., relating either to the intestinal microflora (total fat, fiber, fermented milk products).

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: 133 breast cancer cases and 289 population controls in The Netherlands.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: This resulted in an age-adjusted odds ratio of 0.40 (95% CI = 0.14 - 1.15), which was largely attributable to the combination of low intake of fat and high intake of fermented milk products and fiber.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: high intake of fermented milk products and fiber

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger's test indicates no significant funnel plot asymmetry (p=0.0523). The distribution of studies appears symmetric, suggesting a lower risk of publication bias.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 7 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.54 (95% CI: 0.37–0.78), suggesting that non-alcoholic fermented foods is associated with a lower risk of breast cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 67.77%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
